opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this was one of the findings that surprised us most when we started tracing what's going on inside the model.

The intuitive story you might expect is that the model tries to recall facts about a person, and if it comes up empty, it says "I don't know." What we actually found looks closer to the reverse. There's a default circuit that's on by default, essentially "I can't answer this," "I don't know who this is." Then, when the model recognizes an entity it knows a lot about, say Michael Jordan, a set of "known entity" features activate and inhibit that default. They suppress the "I don't know" pathway, and that lets the model go ahead and answer.

If you ask about someone made up, say Michael Batkin, nothing fires strongly enough to suppress the default, so the model declines. That's a pretty sensible design in a way: skepticism is the baseline, and familiarity has to earn the right to answer.

It also gives you a mechanistic story for some hallucinations. If the "I know this" signal fires but the actual facts aren't there, you get a misfire. Maybe the name is vaguely familiar, or you've seen it in a paper title but don't actually know what the person did. The model has suppressed its own "I don't know" response but has nothing real to say, so it confabulates something plausible. We could reproduce that: by artificially activating the known-entity features, we got the model to confidently hallucinate about a made-up name. Conversely, by inhibiting them, we got it to decline on things it actually knows.

So how do I assess it? I think it's reasonable as a first-order mechanism, and it's a big part of why newer models hallucinate less than older ones. But it's somewhat decoupled from the actual retrieval. Recognition and recall are separate signals, and when they disagree, that's where you get errors. That's useful to know, both for understanding the failure mode and for thinking about how you might train or monitor for it. You could imagine watching that gap directly rather than just checking outputs after the fact.

r001.rationale: It says a default circuit is active for “I can’t answer” or “I don’t know who this is,” and that the model declines when nothing suppresses it.

r002.rationale: It explains that recognizing a known entity activates separate “known entity” features, which inhibit the default “I don’t know” pathway.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite case studies, actually, because it's a place where the mechanism looks almost nothing like what you'd intuitively guess.

So the setup: you ask Claude about a person. Michael Jordan, say, versus some name it's never seen, like "Michael Batkin." For Jordan it'll tell you he plays basketball. For Batkin, it'll say, "I'm sorry, I don't recognize that person." And the naive story is that the model somehow checks, "do I have facts about this entity?" and then decides. That's not what we found.

What we found is that the default behavior is refusal. There's a set of features in the middle of the network that you could describe as "unknown entity" or "can't answer" features, and they are on by default for any name-shaped thing. When the model recognizes an entity it actually knows a lot about, there's a separate "known entity" feature that fires, and it actively inhibits the refusal circuit. So knowing isn't what triggers answering. Not-knowing isn't what triggers refusing. There's a refusal that runs unless something suppresses it, and familiarity is what suppresses it.

The reason I find that elegant is that it's actually a pretty reasonable design from a training perspective. Pre-training teaches the model to just complete the text, and it'll happily complete text about Michael Batkin with plausible-sounding nonsense. Fine-tuning then has to bolt on "don't do that," and the cheapest way to do that is a blanket default of "I don't know this," plus an override for the cases where it clearly does.

And then the assessment part, which is really your question: how good is this mechanism? The honest answer is it's good but it's a proxy. The "known entity" feature is tracking something like "is this a familiar name," not "do I actually have the specific fact being asked about." And those two things come apart. We saw this with a case where you ask about a paper by an author Claude recognizes. The author is famous enough that the known-entity feature fires, the refusal gets suppressed, and now the model is committed to answering. But it doesn't actually know the paper's title. So it confabulates one. It's a hallucination, and when you look under the hood, it's this exact misfire: the familiarity gate opened, but the knowledge wasn't there behind it.

We could even cause it directly. If you take the Batkin prompt and artificially turn up the "known answer" feature, the model will cheerfully tell you Batkin plays chess or whatever. You've overridden the refusal with a fake confidence signal.

So my assessment would be: it's a surprisingly sensible architecture, it explains a real pattern of failures, and it's more legible than I expected. But the thing it's checking is one step removed from the thing we actually want it to check. The ideal would be a mechanism that reads out confidence about the specific claim, not about the entity in general. Whether you can train that in, or whether it's fundamentally a limitation of how these models store knowledge, I think is still genuinely open. And I'd be careful about over-generalizing from one case study. This is one circuit, in one model, under one kind of probe. The broader lesson I take from it is less "now we understand hallucination" and more "the mechanism is often not the one you'd write down from the behavior alone, and you have to go look."

r001.rationale: The response says refusal is the default for any name-shaped thing, with an “I don’t know” response unless that refusal is suppressed.

r002.rationale: It explains that a separate known-entity feature fires for a familiar person and actively inhibits the default refusal circuit.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: does it actually know enough about the person, and can it reliably recognize when it doesn’t? Those aren’t necessarily the same capability. A model can produce a very confident, plausible biography without having enough information to support it.

So I’d assess the mechanism behaviorally. Give it questions about people it can identify reliably, people it knows very little about, and names that are ambiguous. Then look at when it answers, when it asks for clarification, and when it says it doesn’t know. You want its willingness to answer to track its actual accuracy. Just asking the model whether it feels confident isn’t enough; you have to check whether that confidence predicts correctness.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that Claude defaults to refusing questions about a person; it discusses testing when the model answers or says it does not know.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe name or context features triggering a separate circuit that inhibits a default “I don’t know” response.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two separate questions there. One is whether Claude can tell you something about a person, and the other is whether it can reliably judge that what it’s telling you is correct. Those aren’t necessarily the same capability. A model can produce a very plausible biography without having enough information to support it.

So I’d assess that mechanism empirically. Give it people it knows a lot about, people it knows very little about, and names that are ambiguous, and see when it answers, when it asks for clarification, and when it says it doesn’t know. You want it to be helpful when it has enough information, but you also want its willingness to answer to track its actual accuracy. The fact that it sounds confident—or can explain why it thinks it knows—isn’t sufficient evidence that the mechanism works.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing whether Claude answers, asks for clarification, or says it doesn’t know, but does not state that it defaults to refusing person-related questions.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe name or context features triggering a separate circuit that inhibits a default “I don’t know” response.
